q-32876.name: Question 1
q-32876.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k$ at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2}),$ valid for real values of $u?$
q-32876.worked_solution:
The point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t=0 \\ t=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{3}{2}).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,j+\,k \\  & =0\,i+\pi \,j+\,k \\  & =\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is

$$
R(u)=-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u\,(\pi \,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 1

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=sin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj+tk at the point P(−1,0,32), valid for real values of u?

a
−i+32k+u(i+πj+k)
b
−i−32k+u(πi+k)
c
−i+32k+u(−πj−k)
d
−i+32k+u(πj+k)
e
−i+32k+u(πi+j)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The point P(−1,0,32) is at the tip of r(t) for some specific value t0 of the parameter t. At this point, the vector r′(t0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(t0)+ur′(t0),u∈(−∞,∞).

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to P. We know that

r(t)=−i+0j+32ksin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj+tk=−i+0j+32k,

and equating the coefficients of i,j, and k yields the following system:

{sin⁡πt=−1cos⁡πt=0t=32.

From the first equation, we get t=32. This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, P(−1,0,32) is at the tip of the vector r(32).

We calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡πt)i+ddt(cos⁡πt)j+ddt(t)k=πcos⁡πti−πsin⁡πtj+k

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=32:

r′(32)=πcos⁡(3π2)i−πsin⁡(3π2)j+k=0i+πj+k=πj+k

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point P(−1,0,32) is R(u)=−i+32k+u(πj+k),u∈(−∞,∞).

q-75521.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
q-75521.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j]\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1-\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{{t}^{2}} & =0 \\ t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}} & =0 \\ {t}^{4} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1)=1\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j=\,i+j, \\ r(-1)=(-1)\,i+\frac{1}{(-1)}\,j=-\,i-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)+5,1-{0}^{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨5,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+5),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨3,-3(0)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨5,1⟩+u⟨3,0⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

q-126901.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨4t-{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩,$ find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨2,1⟩.$
q-126901.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$

q-165042.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
q-165042.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$
